claim: Striatal cholinergic interneurons (SCINs) exhibit pause responses conveying information about rewarding events.
source: Striatal cholinergic interneurons (SCINs) exhibit pause responses conveying information about rewarding events, but the mechanisms underlying these pauses remain elusive.
evidence: This is a statement of established scientific knowledge about SCIN function.

claim: Thalamic inputs induce a pause in SCINs mediated by intrinsic mechanisms.
source: Thalamic inputs induce a pause mediated by intrinsic mechanisms and regulated by dopamine D2 receptors (D2Rs), though the underlying membrane currents remain unknown.
evidence: This is supported by citations to prior work and the experimental data presented in the manuscript.

claim: The SCIN pause is regulated by dopamine D2 receptors (D2Rs).
source: Thalamic inputs induce a pause mediated by intrinsic mechanisms and regulated by dopamine D2 receptors (D2Rs), though the underlying membrane currents remain unknown.
evidence: This is supported by citations to prior work and experimental data in the manuscript.

claim: The underlying membrane currents mediating the SCIN pause remain unknown.
source: Thalamic inputs induce a pause mediated by intrinsic mechanisms and regulated by dopamine D2 receptors (D2Rs), though the underlying membrane currents remain unknown.
evidence: This is a statement about the state of knowledge prior to this study.

claim: The role of D5 receptors (D5Rs) in the SCIN pause has not been addressed.
source: Moreover, the role of D5 receptors (D5Rs) has not been addressed so far.
evidence: This is a statement about the state of knowledge prior to this study.

claim: Glutamate released by thalamic inputs in the dorsolateral striatum induces a burst in SCINs followed by a pause.
source: Here, we performed ex vivo studies showing that glutamate released by thalamic inputs in the dorsolateral striatum induces a burst in SCINs, followed by a pause mediated by the activation of a Kv1-dependent delayed rectifier current.
evidence: This is supported by experimental data presented in the manuscript, including optogenetic stimulation experiments and pharmacological blockade with CNQX.

claim: The SCIN pause following thalamic input is mediated by the activation of a Kv1-dependent delayed rectifier current.
source: Here, we performed ex vivo studies showing that glutamate released by thalamic inputs in the dorsolateral striatum induces a burst in SCINs, followed by a pause mediated by the activation of a Kv1-dependent delayed rectifier current.
evidence: This is supported by experimental data showing that Kv1 channel blockers (MgTx and DTx) abolish the pause.

claim: Endogenous dopamine promotes the SCIN pause through D2R stimulation.
source: Endogenous dopamine promotes this pause through D2R stimulation, while pharmacological stimulation of D5Rs suppresses it.
evidence: This is supported by experimental data showing effects of D2R antagonists and agonists.

claim: Pharmacological stimulation of D5Rs suppresses the SCIN pause.
source: Endogenous dopamine promotes this pause through D2R stimulation, while pharmacological stimulation of D5Rs suppresses it.
evidence: This is supported by experimental data showing that SKF81297 (D1/D5R agonist) suppresses the pause.

claim: The SCIN pause is absent in parkinsonian mice rendered dyskinetic by chronic L-DOPA treatment.
source: Remarkably, this pause is absent in parkinsonian mice rendered dyskinetic by chronic L-DOPA treatment but can be reinstated acutely by the inverse D5R agonist clozapine.
evidence: This is supported by experimental data from recordings in dyskinetic mice.

claim: The SCIN pause can be reinstated in dyskinetic mice by the inverse D5R agonist clozapine.
source: Remarkably, this pause is absent in parkinsonian mice rendered dyskinetic by chronic L-DOPA treatment but can be reinstated acutely by the inverse D5R agonist clozapine.
evidence: This is supported by experimental data showing clozapine restores the pause in dyskinetic mice.

claim: Blocking the Kv1 current eliminates the pause reinstated by the D5R inverse agonist in dyskinetic mice.
source: Blocking the Kv1 current eliminates the pause reinstated by the D5R inverse agonist.
evidence: This is supported by experimental data showing MgTx blocks the clozapine effect.

claim: D2-type receptor agonists quinpirole and sumanirole failed to reinstate a pause in dyskinetic mice.
source: In contrast, the D2-type receptor agonists quinpirole and sumanirole failed to reinstate a pause in dyskinetic mice.
evidence: This is supported by experimental data from pharmacological experiments in dyskinetic mice.

claim: The SCIN pause is lost in parkinsonian mice that have been rendered dyskinetic.
source: In conclusion, stimulation of thalamic inputs induces excitation followed by a pause in SCINs, which is lost in parkinsonian mice that have been rendered dyskinetic.
evidence: This is supported by experimental data from recordings in dyskinetic mice.

claim: The SCIN pause is mediated by delayed rectifier Kv1 channels.
source: This pause is mediated by delayed rectifier Kv1 channels, which are tonically blocked in dyskinetic mice by a mechanism depending on D5R ligand-independent activity.
evidence: This is supported by experimental data showing Kv1 blockers eliminate the pause and clozapine restores it.

claim: Kv1 channels are tonically blocked in dyskinetic mice by a mechanism depending on D5R ligand-independent activity.
source: This pause is mediated by delayed rectifier Kv1 channels, which are tonically blocked in dyskinetic mice by a mechanism depending on D5R ligand-independent activity.
evidence: This is supported by experimental data showing D5R inverse agonists restore the pause and prior work on D5R constitutive activity.

claim: Dopamine is released by neurons from the ventral tegmental area and substantia nigra pars compacta (SNc).
source: Dopamine (DA), released by neurons from the ventral tegmental area and substantia nigra pars compacta (SNc), and acetylcholine (ACh), mainly released by striatal cholinergic interneurons (SCINs), are the main modulators of cortico-striatal circuits.
evidence: This is established scientific knowledge about dopaminergic neuron anatomy.

claim: Acetylcholine is mainly released by striatal cholinergic interneurons (SCINs).
source: Dopamine (DA), released by neurons from the ventral tegmental area and substantia nigra pars compacta (SNc), and acetylcholine (ACh), mainly released by striatal cholinergic interneurons (SCINs), are the main modulators of cortico-striatal circuits.
evidence: This is established scientific knowledge about cholinergic neuron function.

claim: Dopamine and acetylcholine are the main modulators of cortico-striatal circuits.
source: Dopamine (DA), released by neurons from the ventral tegmental area and substantia nigra pars compacta (SNc), and acetylcholine (ACh), mainly released by striatal cholinergic interneurons (SCINs), are the main modulators of cortico-striatal circuits.
evidence: This is established scientific knowledge about striatal circuit modulation.

claim: Dopaminergic neurons and SCINs are tonically active.
source: Both types of neurons are tonically active, and their activity is altered by unexpected rewards or by the sensory cues that predict those rewards.
evidence: This is established scientific knowledge about the firing patterns of these neurons.

claim: The activity of dopaminergic neurons and SCINs is altered by unexpected rewards or by sensory cues that predict those rewards.
source: Both types of neurons are tonically active, and their activity is altered by unexpected rewards or by the sensory cues that predict those rewards.
evidence: This is established scientific knowledge about reward-related neural responses.

claim: Unexpected rewards or predictive sensory cues evoke a burst in dopaminergic neurons coincident with a pause response in SCINs.
source: These events evoke a burst in dopaminergic neurons coincident with a pause response in SCINs.
evidence: This is established scientific knowledge about coordinated neural responses to rewards.

claim: The increase in DA and decrease in ACh following reward-related events are critical for striatal-dependent learning and decision-making.
source: The resulting increase in DA and decrease in ACh are critical for striatal-dependent learning and decision-making through modulatory effects on striatal 'medium spiny' projection neurons (MSNs) (Cragg, 2006; Ding et al., 2010; Reynolds et al., 2022).
evidence: This is supported by citations to prior work.

claim: The phasic response of striatal tonically active neurons (TANs, putative SCINs) to salient events typically involves a brief burst of action potentials followed by a short pause.
source: In vivo recordings show that the phasic response of striatal tonically active neurons (TANs, putative SCINs) to salient events typically involves a brief burst of action potentials followed by a short pause (Kimura et al., 1984; Aosaki et al., 1994a; Aosaki et al., 1994b; Apicella, 2007).
evidence: This is supported by citations to prior in vivo recording studies.

claim: The SCIN pause response varies across striatal subregions.
source: Recent in vivo studies in rodents show variations in the SCIN pause response across striatal subregions, where the initial excitation preceding the pause is typically seen in the dorsolateral striatum but may be minimal or absent in the dorsomedial region (Duhne et al., 2024).
evidence: This is supported by citation to a recent study.

claim: The initial excitation preceding the pause is typically seen in the dorsolateral striatum but may be minimal or absent in the dorsomedial region.
source: Recent in vivo studies in rodents show variations in the SCIN pause response across striatal subregions, where the initial excitation preceding the pause is typically seen in the dorsolateral striatum but may be minimal or absent in the dorsomedial region (Duhne et al., 2024).
evidence: This is supported by citation to a recent study.

claim: Neurons of the intralaminar nuclei of the thalamus send excitatory projections to the striatum.
source: Neurons of the intralaminar nuclei of the thalamus, which send excitatory projections to the striatum, also respond to reward and salient stimuli, and the TAN pause is absent when the thalamus is locally inhibited (Matsumoto et al., 2001).
evidence: This is established anatomical knowledge supported by citation.

claim: Neurons of the intralaminar nuclei of the thalamus respond to reward and salient stimuli.
source: Neurons of the intralaminar nuclei of the thalamus, which send excitatory projections to the striatum, also respond to reward and salient stimuli, and the TAN pause is absent when the thalamus is locally inhibited (Matsumoto et al., 2001).
evidence: This is supported by citation to prior work.

claim: The TAN pause is absent when the thalamus is locally inhibited.
source: Neurons of the intralaminar nuclei of the thalamus, which send excitatory projections to the striatum, also respond to reward and salient stimuli, and the TAN pause is absent when the thalamus is locally inhibited (Matsumoto et al., 2001).
evidence: This is supported by citation to prior experimental work.

claim: Dopamine D2 receptor (D2R) antagonists reduce the duration of the pause.
source: Dopamine D2 receptor (D2R) antagonists or genetic elimination of D2Rs from cholinergic neurons have been shown to reduce the duration of the pause (Watanabe and Kimura, 1998; Ding et al., 2010; Kharkwal et al., 2016), implicating a direct contribution of D2R-mediated inhibition of SCINs.
evidence: This is supported by citations to prior work.

claim: Genetic elimination of D2Rs from cholinergic neurons reduces the duration of the pause.
source: Dopamine D2 receptor (D2R) antagonists or genetic elimination of D2Rs from cholinergic neurons have been shown to reduce the duration of the pause (Watanabe and Kimura, 1998; Ding et al., 2010; Kharkwal et al., 2016), implicating a direct contribution of D2R-mediated inhibition of SCINs.
evidence: This is supported by citations to prior work.

claim: Ex vivo studies reveal heterogeneous responses of SCINs to stimulation of dopaminergic axons.
source: Additionally, ex vivo studies reveal heterogeneous responses of SCINs to stimulation of dopaminergic axons, with a more pronounced dopaminergic influence on the pause response in the dorsal vs the ventral striatum (Chuhma et al., 2014).
evidence: This is supported by citation to prior work.

claim: There is a more pronounced dopaminergic influence on the pause response in the dorsal vs the ventral striatum.
source: Additionally, ex vivo studies reveal heterogeneous responses of SCINs to stimulation of dopaminergic axons, with a more pronounced dopaminergic influence on the pause response in the dorsal vs the ventral striatum (Chuhma et al., 2014).
evidence: This is supported by citation to prior work.

claim: The pause in SCINs arises from intrinsic mechanisms activated by depolarization.
source: Further evidence suggests that the pause in SCINs arises from intrinsic mechanisms activated by depolarization (Reynolds et al., 2004; Wilson and Goldberg, 2006; Sanchez et al., 2011).
evidence: This is supported by citations to prior work.

claim: The pause that follows stimulation of SCIN excitatory inputs persists after blocking GABA-A receptors.
source: Experiments conducted in brain slices demonstrate that the pause that follows stimulation of SCIN excitatory inputs persists even after blocking GABA-A receptors, indicating the involvement of voltage (Kv) or calcium-dependent (KCa) potassium currents, with DA likely modulating these currents (Ding et al., 2010; Schulz and Reynolds, 2013; Zhang et al., 2018; McGuirt et al., 2022).
evidence: This is supported by citations to prior work.

claim: The SCIN pause involves voltage (Kv) or calcium-dependent (KCa) potassium currents.
source: Experiments conducted in brain slices demonstrate that the pause that follows stimulation of SCIN excitatory inputs persists even after blocking GABA-A receptors, indicating the involvement of voltage (Kv) or calcium-dependent (KCa) potassium currents, with DA likely modulating these currents (Ding et al., 2010; Schulz and Reynolds, 2013; Zhang et al., 2018; McGuirt et al., 2022).
evidence: This is supported by citations to prior work and inference from experimental results.

claim: DA likely modulates the potassium currents involved in the SCIN pause.
source: Experiments conducted in brain slices demonstrate that the pause that follows stimulation of SCIN excitatory inputs persists even after blocking GABA-A receptors, indicating the involvement of voltage (Kv) or calcium-dependent (KCa) potassium currents, with DA likely modulating these currents (Ding et al., 2010; Schulz and Reynolds, 2013; Zhang et al., 2018; McGuirt et al., 2022).
evidence: This is supported by citations to prior work and inference from experimental results.

claim: The pause is absent in animals with chronic nigrostriatal lesions.
source: The importance of DA is underscored by the absence of pause in animals with chronic nigrostriatal lesions (Aosaki et al., 1994a).
evidence: This is supported by citation to prior work.

claim: Genetic elimination of D2Rs from cholinergic neurons reduces but does not eliminate the pause.
source: While reduced D2R stimulation may explain this, genetic elimination of D2Rs from cholinergic neurons reduces but does not eliminate the pause (Kharkwal et al., 2016), suggesting that additional factors are involved.
evidence: This is supported by citation to prior work.

claim: Additional factors beyond D2Rs are involved in the SCIN pause.
source: While reduced D2R stimulation may explain this, genetic elimination of D2Rs from cholinergic neurons reduces but does not eliminate the pause (Kharkwal et al., 2016), suggesting that additional factors are involved.
evidence: This is inferred from the observation that D2R elimination does not completely abolish the pause.

claim: SCINs express dopamine D5 receptors (D5Rs).
source: SCINs also express dopamine D5 receptors (D5Rs), which have been recently linked to SCIN functional changes in parkinsonian animals (Paz et al., 2022).
evidence: This is supported by citation to prior work.

claim: D5Rs have been recently linked to SCIN functional changes in parkinsonian animals.
source: SCINs also express dopamine D5 receptors (D5Rs), which have been recently linked to SCIN functional changes in parkinsonian animals (Paz et al., 2022).
evidence: This is supported by citation to prior work.

claim: The latency of the evoked spike decreased with the time separating the stimulus from the preceding spontaneous spike.
source: When the stimulation elicited a minimal response (1 spike), the latency of the evoked spike decreased with the time separating the stimulus from the preceding spontaneous spike (Figure 1D and E).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1D and E.

claim: A stimulus arriving after an average baseline interspike interval (ISI) has elapsed produces a shorter latency response than a stimulus arriving shortly after the preceding spontaneous spike.
source: Thus, a stimulus arriving after an average baseline interspike interval (ISI) has elapsed produces a shorter latency response than a stimulus arriving shortly after the preceding spontaneous spike (Figure 1E), as expected given the strong after-hyperpolarization (AHP) that follows SCIN spikes (Reynolds et al., 2004; Wilson and Goldberg, 2006).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data in Figure 1E and citations to prior work on SCIN AHP.

claim: A strong after-hyperpolarization (AHP) follows SCIN spikes.
source: Thus, a stimulus arriving after an average baseline interspike interval (ISI) has elapsed produces a shorter latency response than a stimulus arriving shortly after the preceding spontaneous spike (Figure 1E), as expected given the strong after-hyperpolarization (AHP) that follows SCIN spikes (Reynolds et al., 2004; Wilson and Goldberg, 2006).
evidence: This is supported by citations to prior work.

claim: After optical stimulation, the response latencies were significantly smaller at intervals shorter and longer than the average ISI, indicating that the stimulation increased spike probability.
source: While a similar inverse relationship is observed under conditions of 'sham stimulation' (Figure 1E), after optical stimulation, the response latencies were significantly smaller at intervals shorter and longer than the average ISI, indicating that the stimulation increased spike probability (Figure 1F).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1F.

claim: The interval that followed minimal responses (1 spike) was 30% longer than the average ISI.
source: Remarkably, the interval that followed these minimal responses was 30% longer than the average ISI (baseline ISI: 464.61±42.44 ms; pause after 1 elicited spike: 609.3±59.5; p=0.0181, paired t-test), indicating that even an initial excitatory response consisting in a single spike delays the next SCIN spike.
evidence: This is supported by experimental data with statistical analysis.

claim: Even an initial excitatory response consisting in a single spike delays the next SCIN spike.
source: Remarkably, the interval that followed these minimal responses was 30% longer than the average ISI (baseline ISI: 464.61±42.44 ms; pause after 1 elicited spike: 609.3±59.5; p=0.0181, paired t-test), indicating that even an initial excitatory response consisting in a single spike delays the next SCIN spike.
evidence: This is inferred from the experimental data showing increased ISI after stimulation.

claim: The burst-pause response to optogenetic activation of thalamic terminals was abolished by application of an AMPA receptor antagonist.
source: By increasing the number of pulses in the stimulation train, we obtained responses of 2–4 spikes ('bursts') followed by an interruption of SCIN firing, which were abolished by application of an AMPA receptor antagonist in the bath (normalized firing rate (burst/baseline): PIC = 3.611; PIC+CNQX = 1.343; paired t-test, p=0.0409; n=5 cells from 5 animals) (Figure 1G).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1G with statistical analysis.

claim: The duration of the SCIN pause increased with the number of spikes in the burst evoked by thalamic stimulation.
source: The duration of the SCIN pause increased with the number of spikes in the burst (Figure 1H), without changes in baseline ISI (Figure 1I), as expected if the pause depended on the recruitment of a depolarization-activated hyperpolarizing current (average pause durations: 1 elicited spike = 609.3±59.5 ms; 2 elicited spikes = 744.2±92.4 ms; 3 elicited spikes = 964.7±92.3 ms; 4 elicited spikes = 1065.7±136.5 ms; baseline ISI: 1 elicited spike = 464.6±42.4 ms; 2 elicited spikes = 427.7±36.3 ms; 3 elicited spikes = 430.5±39.9 ms; 4 elicited spikes = 440.3±53.4 ms).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1H with statistical analysis.

claim: Baseline ISI did not change with the number of spikes in the burst.
source: The duration of the SCIN pause increased with the number of spikes in the burst (Figure 1H), without changes in baseline ISI (Figure 1I), as expected if the pause depended on the recruitment of a depolarization-activated hyperpolarizing current (average pause durations: 1 elicited spike = 609.3±59.5 ms; 2 elicited spikes = 744.2±92.4 ms; 3 elicited spikes = 964.7±92.3 ms; 4 elicited spikes = 1065.7±136.5 ms; baseline ISI: 1 elicited spike = 464.6±42.4 ms; 2 elicited spikes = 427.7±36.3 ms; 3 elicited spikes = 430.5±39.9 ms; 4 elicited spikes = 440.3±53.4 ms).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1I with statistical analysis.

claim: The pause depends on the recruitment of a depolarization-activated hyperpolarizing current.
source: The duration of the SCIN pause increased with the number of spikes in the burst (Figure 1H), without changes in baseline ISI (Figure 1I), as expected if the pause depended on the recruitment of a depolarization-activated hyperpolarizing current (average pause durations: 1 elicited spike = 609.3±59.5 ms; 2 elicited spikes = 744.2±92.4 ms; 3 elicited spikes = 964.7±92.3 ms; 4 elicited spikes = 1065.7±136.5 ms; baseline ISI: 1 elicited spike = 464.6±42.4 ms; 2 elicited spikes = 427.7±36.3 ms; 3 elicited spikes = 430.5±39.9 ms; 4 elicited spikes = 440.3±53.4 ms).
evidence: This is inferred from the experimental observation that pause duration increases with burst size.

claim: Thalamic neurons driving the burst-pause response of SCINs show a burst followed by a pause that ends with a rebound of activity in connection with reward-related events.
source: A pioneering in vivo study showed that the thalamic neurons presumptively driving the burst-pause response of SCINs show a burst followed by a pause that ends with a rebound of activity, in connection with reward-related events.
evidence: This is supported by citation to prior work.

claim: The thalamic burst-pause response temporally coincides with the burst-pause response of the presumptive SCINs.
source: This thalamic burst-pause response temporally coincides with the burst-pause response of the presumptive SCINs (Matsumoto et al., 2001).
evidence: This is supported by citation to prior work.

claim: A decrease in excitatory afferent activity may be necessary for the expression of the SCIN pause.
source: This suggests that a decrease in excitatory afferent activity may be necessary for the expression of the SCIN pause.
evidence: This is inferred from the temporal coincidence of thalamic and SCIN pause responses.

claim: A second stimulus train could terminate the pause, although its effect is delayed as more spikes are recruited in the burst by the first stimulus.
source: We found that the second stimulus train could terminate the pause, although its effect is delayed as more spikes are recruited in the burst by the first stimulus (Figure 1J and K).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1J and K.

claim: The delayed effect of the second stimulus is consistent with a graded recruitment of an intrinsic current that reduces the excitability of SCINs.
source: This is consistent with a graded recruitment of an intrinsic current that reduces the excitability of SCINs, delaying their response to the second stimulus.
evidence: This is inferred from the experimental observation that larger bursts delay the response to a second stimulus.

claim: Kv delayed rectifier channels constituted by Kv1.3 and Kv1.1 subunits contribute to the slow AHP current in SCINs of adult mice.
source: In previous work, we found that Kv delayed rectifier channels constituted by Kv1.3 and Kv1.1 subunits contribute to the slow AHP current in SCINs of adult mice (Tubert et al., 2016).
evidence: This is supported by citation to prior work by the authors.

claim: A train of EPSPs evoked by thalamic afferents stimulation is followed by an AHP, which persists in the presence of the GABA-A receptor antagonist PIC and is blocked by the Kv1.3 channel blocker margatoxin (MgTx).
source: Moreover, a train of EPSPs evoked by thalamic afferents stimulation is followed by an AHP, which persists in the presence of the GABA-A receptor antagonist PIC and is blocked by the Kv1.3 channel blocker margatoxin (MgTx) (Tubert et al., 2016).
evidence: This is supported by citation to prior work by the authors.

claim: MgTx at 30 nM abolished the pause response without changing the spontaneous firing rate or the burst duration.
source: Both MgTx at 30 nM – but not at 3 nM – and dendrotoxin (DTx, 100 nM, a Kv1.1 and Kv1.6 channel blocker) abolished the pause response without changing the spontaneous firing rate or the burst duration (Figure 2A–E).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 2A-E.

claim: MgTx at 3 nM did not abolish the pause response.
source: Both MgTx at 30 nM – but not at 3 nM – and dendrotoxin (DTx, 100 nM, a Kv1.1 and Kv1.6 channel blocker) abolished the pause response without changing the spontaneous firing rate or the burst duration (Figure 2A–E).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 2A-E.

claim: Dendrotoxin (DTx, 100 nM, a Kv1.1 and Kv1.6 channel blocker) abolished the pause response without changing the spontaneous firing rate or the burst duration.
source: Both MgTx at 30 nM – but not at 3 nM – and dendrotoxin (DTx, 100 nM, a Kv1.1 and Kv1.6 channel blocker) abolished the pause response without changing the spontaneous firing rate or the burst duration (Figure 2A–E).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 2A-E.

claim: Kv1.1 and Kv1.3 mRNAs are expressed in SCINs but not in striatal tissue samples lacking SCINs.
source: Previous studies showed that Kv1.1 and Kv1.3 mRNAs are expressed in SCINs but not in striatal tissue samples lacking SCINs (Tubert et al., 2016), consistent with independent findings showing that Kv1.3 mRNA is absent in MSNs (Shen et al., 2004).
evidence: This is supported by citations to prior work.

claim: Kv1.3 mRNA is absent in MSNs.
source: Previous studies showed that Kv1.1 and Kv1.3 mRNAs are expressed in SCINs but not in striatal tissue samples lacking SCINs (Tubert et al., 2016), consistent with independent findings showing that Kv1.3 mRNA is absent in MSNs (Shen et al., 2004).
evidence: This is supported by citation to prior work.

claim: The effect of MgTx on the pause response is likely mediated by direct actions on SCINs.
source: These findings suggest that the effect of MgTx on the pause response is likely mediated by direct actions on SCINs.
evidence: This is inferred from the expression pattern of Kv1 channels in SCINs but not MSNs.

claim: SCINs have a high reserve of Kv7 channels that limit EPSP summation but do not seem to contribute to the slow AHP or pause response in adult mice.
source: SCINs have a high reserve of Kv7 channels that limit EPSP summation but do not seem to contribute to the slow AHP (Paz et al., 2018) or pause response (McGuirt et al., 2022) in adult mice.
evidence: This is supported by citations to prior work.

claim: The pause induced by thalamic stimulation was not reduced by the Kv7 channel blocker XE-991 (10 µM).
source: Consistent with these findings, the pause induced by thalamic stimulation was not reduced by the Kv7 channel blocker XE-991 (10 µM) (Figure 2F–I).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 2F-I.

claim: SCIN hyperpolarizations can be amplified by the recruitment of inwardly rectifying Kir2 channels, presumptively of the Kir2.2 subtype.
source: Moreover, SCIN hyperpolarizations can be amplified by the recruitment of inwardly rectifying Kir2 channels, presumptively of the Kir2.2 subtype (Paz et al., 2021), which could then contribute to the pause response (Figure 2A).
evidence: This is supported by citation to prior work.

claim: A low concentration of barium (10 µM) that preferentially blocks Kir2.2 channels had no effect on firing frequency, burst duration, or pause response of SCINs to thalamic stimulation.
source: However, a low concentration of barium that preferentially blocks Kir2.2 channels (10 µM) had no effect on firing frequency, burst duration, or pause response of SCINs to thalamic stimulation (Figure 2F–I).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 2F-I.

claim: The Kv1 current is necessary for the expression of the pause that follows the stimulation of thalamic inputs in SCINs of adult mice.
source: Overall, the data show that the Kv1 current is necessary for the expression of the pause that follows the stimulation of thalamic inputs in SCINs of adult mice.
evidence: This is supported by experimental data showing Kv1 blockers eliminate the pause.

claim: DA promotes the pause response through D2R-mediated actions.
source: Previous in vivo and ex vivo studies have shown that DA promotes the pause response through D2R-mediated actions (Aosaki et al., 1994a; Watanabe and Kimura, 1998; Deng et al., 2007; Ding et al., 2010), including inhibitory effects on Ih, which could be activated by the pause and contribute to its end (Deng et al., 2007; McGuirt et al., 2022).
evidence: This is supported by citations to prior work.

claim: D2R-mediated actions include inhibitory effects on Ih, which could be activated by the pause and contribute to its end.
source: Previous in vivo and ex vivo studies have shown that DA promotes the pause response through D2R-mediated actions (Aosaki et al., 1994a; Watanabe and Kimura, 1998; Deng et al., 2007; Ding et al., 2010), including inhibitory effects on Ih, which could be activated by the pause and contribute to its end (Deng et al., 2007; McGuirt et al., 2022).
evidence: This is supported by citations to prior work.

claim: The pause shortens when D2R endogenous activation is blocked with D2-type receptor antagonists.
source: The pause shortens when D2R endogenous activation is blocked with D2-type receptor antagonists (Aosaki et al., 1994a; Watanabe and Kimura, 1998; Ding et al., 2010) or D2Rs are genetically eliminated (Kharkwal et al., 2016), and lengthens when D2Rs are overexpressed in SCINs (Gallo et al., 2022).
evidence: This is supported by citations to prior work.

claim: The pause lengthens when D2Rs are overexpressed in SCINs.
source: The pause shortens when D2R endogenous activation is blocked with D2-type receptor antagonists (Aosaki et al., 1994a; Watanabe and Kimura, 1998; Ding et al., 2010) or D2Rs are genetically eliminated (Kharkwal et al., 2016), and lengthens when D2Rs are overexpressed in SCINs (Gallo et al., 2022).
evidence: This is supported by citation to prior work.

claim: D5Rs increase SCIN excitability by reducing the Kv1-mediated delayed rectifier current.
source: In addition to D2Rs, SCINs express D5Rs that increase SCIN excitability by reducing the Kv1-mediated delayed rectifier current (Paz et al., 2021; Paz et al., 2022), shown above to be involved in the pause response.
evidence: This is supported by citations to prior work by the authors.

claim: SKF81297 suppressed the pause without changing SCIN spontaneous firing rate.
source: SKF81297 suppressed this pause without changing SCIN spontaneous firing rate, although there was a trend toward shorter baseline ISIs under SKF81297 alone (Figure 3A–E).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 3A-E.

claim: There was a trend toward shorter baseline ISIs under SKF81297 alone.
source: SKF81297 suppressed this pause without changing SCIN spontaneous firing rate, although there was a trend toward shorter baseline ISIs under SKF81297 alone (Figure 3A–E).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 3A-E.

claim: The effect of SKF81297 was prevented by co-application of the selective D1/D5R antagonist SCH23390.
source: The effect of SKF81297 was prevented by co-application of the selective D1/D5R antagonist SCH23390, which had no effects by itself, ruling out tonic effects of DA through D5Rs (Figure 3A–E).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 3A-E.

claim: SCH23390 had no effects by itself, ruling out tonic effects of DA through D5Rs.
source: The effect of SKF81297 was prevented by co-application of the selective D1/D5R antagonist SCH23390, which had no effects by itself, ruling out tonic effects of DA through D5Rs (Figure 3A–E).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 3A-E and inference from the lack of effect.

claim: There was a small effect of the selective D2R antagonist sulpiride, limited to the pauses that followed 4-spike bursts.
source: Furthermore, we found a small effect of the selective D2R antagonist sulpiride, limited to the pauses that followed 4-spike bursts, supporting a modulatory role of D2Rs (Figure 3F–I).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 3F-I.

claim: Synchronized SCIN bursts induce DA release through local effects mediated by nicotinic receptors located in dopaminergic terminals.
source: Previous studies suggested that synchronized SCIN bursts induce DA release through local effects mediated by nicotinic receptors located in dopaminergic terminals (Threlfell et al., 2012).
evidence: This is supported by citation to prior work.

claim: The nicotinic receptor antagonist mecamylamine reduced the pause that followed 4-spike bursts.
source: Accordingly, the nicotinic receptor antagonist mecamylamine also reduced the pause that followed 4-spike bursts (Figure 3F–I).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 3F-I.

claim: Endogenous levels of DA in the slice are sufficient to stimulate D2Rs but not D5Rs.
source: Presumably, endogenous levels of DA in the slice, produced by tonic release mechanisms or phasic cholinergic activation of dopaminergic terminals, are sufficient to stimulate D2Rs but not D5Rs.
evidence: This is inferred from the differential effects of D2R and D5R antagonists.

claim: ZD7288 blocked HCN channels as shown by the disappearance of the sag induced by hyperpolarizing steps.
source: ZD7288 blocked HCN channels as shown by the disappearance of the sag induced by hyperpolarizing steps (Figure 4B and C).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 4B and C.

claim: HCN channel block stopped spontaneous activity in SCINs.
source: Because HCN channel block also stopped spontaneous activity, we injected current through the electrode to induce spiking.
evidence: This is supported by experimental observation.

claim: Thalamic input stimulation induced a burst-pause response in the presence of ZD7288.
source: In these conditions, thalamic input stimulation induced a burst-pause response.
evidence: This is supported by experimental data.

claim: The suppression of the pause by stimulation of D5Rs with SKF81297 was not prevented by Ih block.
source: Additionally, the suppression of the pause by stimulation of D5Rs with SKF81297 was not prevented by Ih block (Figure 4D–G).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 4D-G.

claim: D5R can inhibit the pause that follows excitation induced by thalamic afferents through effects that are independent of GABA-A receptors, burst amplitude, and Ih current.
source: Our results, so far, extend previous work by showing that D5R can inhibit the pause that follows excitation induced by thalamic afferents through effects that are independent of GABA-A receptors, burst amplitude, and Ih current, likely involving Kv1 current inhibition.
evidence: This is supported by experimental data from the manuscript.

claim: D5R inhibition of the pause likely involves Kv1 current inhibition.
source: Our results, so far, extend previous work by showing that D5R can inhibit the pause that follows excitation induced by thalamic afferents through effects that are independent of GABA-A receptors, burst amplitude, and Ih current, likely involving Kv1 current inhibition.
evidence: This is inferred from the experimental data and prior work on D5R effects on Kv1 channels.

claim: The pause response in putative SCINs is absent in an animal model of Parkinson's disease.
source: Previous in vivo work has shown that the pause response in putative SCINs is absent in an animal model of Parkinson's disease and is partially restored by acute administration of the DA receptor agonist apomorphine (Aosaki et al., 1994a).
evidence: This is supported by citation to prior work.

claim: The pause response is partially restored by acute administration of the DA receptor agonist apomorphine in parkinsonian animals.
source: Previous in vivo work has shown that the pause response in putative SCINs is absent in an animal model of Parkinson's disease and is partially restored by acute administration of the DA receptor agonist apomorphine (Aosaki et al., 1994a).
evidence: This is supported by citation to prior work.

claim: Chronic administration of L-DOPA to parkinsonian animals produces lasting changes in SCIN membrane excitability involving Kv1, Kir2, and likely, other currents.
source: Chronic administration of L-DOPA to parkinsonian animals produces lasting changes in SCIN membrane excitability involving Kv1, Kir2, and likely, other currents (McKinley et al., 2019; Choi et al., 2020; Paz et al., 2021; Paz et al., 2022).
evidence: This is supported by citations to prior work.

claim: Mice unilaterally lesioned with 6-OHDA showed extensive loss of TH-positive neurons in SNc.
source: Mice unilaterally lesioned with 6-OHDA showed extensive loss of TH-positive neurons in SNc (Figure 5B), accompanied by marked parkinsonian-like motor impairment (Figure 5C–E).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 5B.

claim: 6-OHDA lesioned mice showed marked parkinsonian-like motor impairment.
source: Mice unilaterally lesioned with 6-OHDA showed extensive loss of TH-positive neurons in SNc (Figure 5B), accompanied by marked parkinsonian-like motor impairment (Figure 5C–E).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 5C-E.

claim: 6-OHDA lesioned mice developed dyskinesia in response to L-DOPA administration.
source: Moreover, these mice developed dyskinesia in response to L-DOPA administration, characterized by an abnormal involuntary movement (AIM) score that worsens after day 4 of treatment (Figure 5F).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 5F.

claim: The abnormal involuntary movement (AIM) score worsens after day 4 of L-DOPA treatment.
source: Moreover, these mice developed dyskinesia in response to L-DOPA administration, characterized by an abnormal involuntary movement (AIM) score that worsens after day 4 of treatment (Figure 5F).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 5F.

claim: The Kv1 current is diminished after lesioning nigral dopaminergic neurons and further suppressed when recorded 24 hr after the end of a chronic L-DOPA treatment.
source: In previous studies, we have shown that the Kv1 current is diminished after lesioning nigral dopaminergic neurons and further suppressed when recorded 24 hr after the end of a chronic L-DOPA treatment (Paz et al., 2022).
evidence: This is supported by citation to prior work by the authors.

claim: The pause is absent in SCINs from dyskinetic mice recorded 24 hr after the last L-DOPA challenge (OFF L-DOPA condition).
source: Cell-attached recordings performed 24 hr after the last L-DOPA challenge (OFF L-DOPA condition) showed that the pause is absent in SCINs from dyskinetic mice (Figure 5G and H), regardless of the burst duration (Figure 5J).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 5G, H, and J.

claim: The spontaneous firing rate was higher in SCINs recorded from mice in the OFF L-DOPA condition compared with sham mice.
source: Consistent with previous findings (Paz et al., 2021), the spontaneous firing rate was higher in SCINs recorded from mice in the OFF L-DOPA condition compared with sham mice (Figure 5I).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 5I and citation to prior work.

claim: MgTx did not have any effect on pause duration, baseline firing rate, and burst duration in SCINs from dyskinetic mice.
source: In addition, the inclusion of MgTx in the bath did not have any effect on pause duration, baseline firing rate, and burst duration (Figure 5G–J), as expected following previous findings, showing a lack of effect of MgTx on membrane excitability in the same animal model (Paz et al., 2022).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 5G-J and citation to prior work.

claim: A reduction of the Kv1 current is involved in the loss of the pause response in dyskinetic mice.
source: These results support that a reduction of the Kv1 current is involved in the loss of the pause response in dyskinetic mice.
evidence: This is inferred from the experimental data showing loss of pause and lack of MgTx effect in dyskinetic mice.

claim: D2R activation failed to restore the pause response in dyskinetic mice in the OFF L-DOPA condition, either with quinpirole (1 μM) or with the selective D2 agonist sumanirole (10 μM).
source: Contrary to expectations, D2R activation failed to restore the pause response induced by optogenetic stimulation of thalamic afferents, either with quinpirole (1 μM) or with the selective D2 agonist sumanirole (10 μM) (Figure 6A and B).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 6A and B.

claim: Higher concentrations of quinpirole (10 μM) were also ineffective at restoring the pause.
source: Higher concentrations of quinpirole (10 μM) were also ineffective (baseline ISI: OFF L-DOPA=300.8 ± 40 ms, quinpirole = 285.6 ± 40 ms, NS; pause duration/baseline ISI: OFF L-DOPA=1.46 ± 0.18, quinpirole = 1.39 ± 0.16, NS; 14 cells from 5 mice and 3 cells from 3 mice, respectively).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data with statistical analysis.

claim: D2R stimulation had no effect on the spontaneous firing rate of SCINs in dyskinetic mice.
source: In addition, D2R stimulation had no effect on the spontaneous firing rate of SCINs (Figure 6C) or on the duration of burst responses evoked by thalamic input (Figure 6D).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 6C.

claim: D2R stimulation had no effect on the duration of burst responses evoked by thalamic input in dyskinetic mice.
source: In addition, D2R stimulation had no effect on the spontaneous firing rate of SCINs (Figure 6C) or on the duration of burst responses evoked by thalamic input (Figure 6D).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 6D.

claim: D2R stimulation alone is insufficient to restore the SCIN pause in dyskinetic mice.
source: These findings indicate that D2R stimulation alone is insufficient to restore the SCIN pause in dyskinetic mice.
evidence: This is inferred from the experimental data showing lack of effect of D2R agonists.

claim: The physiological changes observed in SCINs of dyskinetic mice depend on increased ligand-independent activity of D5Rs.
source: In a previous study, we found that the physiological changes observed in SCINs of dyskinetic mice depend on increased ligand-independent activity of D5Rs (Paz et al., 2022).
evidence: This is supported by citation to prior work by the authors.

claim: SCINs recorded in the parkinsonian OFF-L-DOPA condition show an increase of membrane excitability that mimics changes acutely induced by SKF81297 in control mice.
source: Paz et al., 2022, recorded SCINs in the parkinsonian OFF-L-DOPA condition and showed an increase of membrane excitability that mimics changes acutely induced by SKF81297 in control mice.
evidence: This is supported by citation to prior work by the authors.

claim: The hyperexcitability phenotype in dyskinetic mice was reversed by acute administration of drugs that reduce D5R ligand-independent activity (i.e. inverse agonists such as clozapine or flupentixol).
source: This hyperexcitability phenotype was reversed by acute administration of drugs that reduce D5R ligand-independent activity (i.e. inverse agonists such as clozapine or flupentixol), as well as by acutely reducing intracellular cAMP signaling (Paz et al., 2022).
evidence: This is supported by citation to prior work by the authors.

claim: The hyperexcitability of SCINs recorded in the OFF L-DOPA condition was not further enhanced by SKF81297 or MgTx.
source: Interestingly, the hyperexcitability of SCINs recorded in the OFF L-DOPA condition was not further enhanced by SKF81297 or MgTx (Paz et al., 2022), suggesting D5R-cAMP-Kv1 inhibitory signaling is already working at full steam in these cells.
evidence: This is supported by citation to prior work by the authors.

claim: D5R-cAMP-Kv1 inhibitory signaling is already working at full steam in SCINs from dyskinetic mice.
source: Interestingly, the hyperexcitability of SCINs recorded in the OFF L-DOPA condition was not further enhanced by SKF81297 or MgTx (Paz et al., 2022), suggesting D5R-cAMP-Kv1 inhibitory signaling is already working at full steam in these cells.
evidence: This is inferred from the lack of additional effect of SKF81297 or MgTx.

claim: Clozapine behaves as an antagonist of D1/D5 and other DA receptors when an agonist is present.
source: The atypical antipsychotic clozapine behaves as an antagonist of D1/D5 and other DA receptors when an agonist is present, but has inverse agonist effects on D5Rs in the absence of an agonist (Zhang et al., 2014).
evidence: This is supported by citation to prior work.

claim: Clozapine has inverse agonist effects on D5Rs in the absence of an agonist.
source: The atypical antipsychotic clozapine behaves as an antagonist of D1/D5 and other DA receptors when an agonist is present, but has inverse agonist effects on D5Rs in the absence of an agonist (Zhang et al., 2014).
evidence: This is supported by citation to prior work.

claim: Clozapine restores the pause in SCINs from dyskinetic mice without changing their firing rate and regardless of the burst duration.
source: Remarkably, clozapine restores the pause in SCINs from dyskinetic mice without changing their firing rate and regardless of the burst duration (Figure 7A–E).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 7A-E.

claim: SCH23390 alone had no effect in the SCIN response to thalamic stimulation in dyskinetic mice.
source: We found that SCH23390 alone had no effect in the SCIN response to thalamic stimulation, as expected given its lack of inverse agonist effects (Tiberi and Caron, 1994) and the DA-depleted condition of the slice preparation.
evidence: This is supported by experimental data and citations to prior work.

claim: SCH23390 prevented the pause-restoring effect of clozapine.
source: However, SCH23390 prevented the pause-restoring effect of clozapine (Figure 7A–E), indicating that engagement of D1/D5Rs is required.
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 7A-E.

claim: Engagement of D1/D5Rs is required for the pause-restoring effect of clozapine.
source: However, SCH23390 prevented the pause-restoring effect of clozapine (Figure 7A–E), indicating that engagement of D1/D5Rs is required.
evidence: This is inferred from the experimental data showing SCH23390 blocks clozapine's effect.

claim: Methiothepin did not block the effect of clozapine, arguing against a serotonergic mechanism.
source: Because clozapine also binds to serotonin receptors (5-HTR), we repeated the experiments in the presence of the broad-spectrum 5-HTR antagonist methiothepin. Methiothepin did not block the effect of clozapine (Figure 7A–E), arguing against a serotonergic mechanism.
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 7A-E.

claim: MgTx occluded the pause-restoring effect of clozapine.
source: Finally, to confirm that the pause restored by clozapine involves Kv1 channels, we co-applied clozapine and MgTx to the bath (Figure 7A). MgTx occluded the pause-restoring effect of clozapine (Figure 7B–E), indicating that reducing D5R ligand-independent activity reinstates the Kv1 current in SCINs from OFF L-DOPA parkinsonian mice.
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 7A-E.

claim: Reducing D5R ligand-independent activity reinstates the Kv1 current in SCINs from OFF L-DOPA parkinsonian mice.
source: Finally, to confirm that the pause restored by clozapine involves Kv1 channels, we co-applied clozapine and MgTx to the bath (Figure 7A). MgTx occluded the pause-restoring effect of clozapine (Figure 7B–E), indicating that reducing D5R ligand-independent activity reinstates the Kv1 current in SCINs from OFF L-DOPA parkinsonian mice.
evidence: This is inferred from the experimental data showing MgTx blocks the clozapine effect.

claim: Theories implicating deactivation of Ih current as the primary cause of the pause were refuted by experiments demonstrating pause induction after Ih current blockade provided the resulting hyperpolarization is compensated by current injection.
source: Theories implicating deactivation of Ih current as its primary cause were refuted by experiments demonstrating pause induction after Ih current blockade provided the resulting hyperpolarization is compensated by current injection (Zhang et al., 2018; present findings).
evidence: This is supported by citation to prior work and experimental data in the manuscript.

claim: Ih likely contributes to a rebound depolarization limiting pause duration.
source: Although Ih likely contributes to a rebound depolarization limiting pause duration (Deng et al., 2007; McGuirt et al., 2022), it does not appear to be essential for pause initiation.
evidence: This is supported by citations to prior work.

claim: Ih does not appear to be essential for pause initiation.
source: Although Ih likely contributes to a rebound depolarization limiting pause duration (Deng et al., 2007; McGuirt et al., 2022), it does not appear to be essential for pause initiation.
evidence: This is inferred from experimental data showing pause persists after Ih blockade.

claim: A slow current mediated by Kv7 channels is involved in the pause in juvenile mice.
source: Further work suggested the involvement of a slow current mediated by Kv7 channels in juvenile mice (Zhang et al., 2018), but this current is developmentally downregulated and does not seem to contribute significantly in adult SCINs (McGuirt et al., 2022; present findings), even though SCINs retain a high reserve of Kv7 channels that remain responsive to pharmacological activators (Paz et al., 2018).
evidence: This is supported by citation to prior work.

claim: The Kv7 current is developmentally downregulated and does not seem to contribute significantly in adult SCINs.
source: Further work suggested the involvement of a slow current mediated by Kv7 channels in juvenile mice (Zhang et al., 2018), but this current is developmentally downregulated and does not seem to contribute significantly in adult SCINs (McGuirt et al., 2022; present findings), even though SCINs retain a high reserve of Kv7 channels that remain responsive to pharmacological activators (Paz et al., 2018).
evidence: This is supported by citations to prior work and experimental data in the manuscript.

claim: SCINs retain a high reserve of Kv7 channels that remain responsive to pharmacological activators.
source: Further work suggested the involvement of a slow current mediated by Kv7 channels in juvenile mice (Zhang et al., 2018), but this current is developmentally downregulated and does not seem to contribute significantly in adult SCINs (McGuirt et al., 2022; present findings), even though SCINs retain a high reserve of Kv7 channels that remain responsive to pharmacological activators (Paz et al., 2018).
evidence: This is supported by citation to prior work.

claim: MgTx enhances subthreshold EPSP summation in SCINs.
source: In SCINs, MgTx enhances subthreshold EPSP summation and blocks the subsequent AHP (Tubert et al., 2016).
evidence: This is supported by citation to prior work by the authors.

claim: Specific blockers of channels constituted by Kv1.3 and Kv1.1 subunits suppress the pause that follows action potential bursts induced by thalamostriatal inputs in adult mice.
source: The present study extends these findings by showing that specific blockers of channels constituted by Kv1.3 and Kv1.1 subunits suppress the pause that follows action potential bursts induced by thalamostriatal inputs in adult mice.
evidence: This is supported by experimental data in the manuscript.

claim: SCINs express inwardly rectifying Kir2 channels capable of amplifying hyperpolarizations.
source: Although SCINs express inwardly rectifying Kir2 channels capable of amplifying hyperpolarizations (Wilson, 2005; Paz et al., 2021), our findings suggest they do not contribute to the pause, likely because of insufficient membrane hyperpolarization to recruit Kir currents.
evidence: This is supported by citations to prior work.

claim: Kir2 channels do not contribute to the pause, likely because of insufficient membrane hyperpolarization to recruit Kir currents.
source: Although SCINs express inwardly rectifying Kir2 channels capable of amplifying hyperpolarizations (Wilson, 2005; Paz et al., 2021), our findings suggest they do not contribute to the pause, likely because of insufficient membrane hyperpolarization to recruit Kir currents.
evidence: This is inferred from experimental data showing no effect of Kir2 blockade on the pause.

claim: The duration of the SCIN pause response is shaped by thalamic inputs.
source: Remarkably, the duration of the SCIN pause response is not only dependent on intrinsic mechanisms but also shaped by thalamic inputs.
evidence: This is supported by experimental data showing effects of second stimulus trains.

claim: SCIN spontaneous firing synchronizes with excitatory synaptic input fluctuations in vivo.
source: In vivo, SCIN spontaneous firing synchronizes with excitatory synaptic input fluctuations (Krok et al., 2023).
evidence: This is supported by citation to prior work.

claim: The phasic SCIN response may reflect synchronization with thalamic inputs, which themselves exhibit a burst-pause-rebound firing pattern in response to reward-related stimuli in vivo.
source: The phasic SCIN response may reflect synchronization with thalamic inputs, which themselves exhibit a burst-pause-rebound firing pattern in response to reward-related stimuli in vivo (Matsumoto et al., 2001).
evidence: This is supported by citation to prior work and inference.

claim: A significant pause could be detected even when only a single spike was evoked by thalamic afferent stimulation.
source: Importantly, a significant pause could be detected even when only a single spike was evoked by thalamic afferent stimulation.
evidence: This is supported by experimental data in the manuscript.

claim: SCIN Kv1 currents are recruited by thalamic input trains that elicit subthreshold depolarizing responses, leading to an AHP.
source: This finding aligns with previous studies showing that SCIN Kv1 currents are recruited by thalamic input trains that elicit subthreshold depolarizing responses, leading to an AHP (Tubert et al., 2016).
evidence: This is supported by citation to prior work by the authors.

claim: SCIN pauses are not always preceded by a burst of spikes in behaving animals.
source: This is particularly interesting given that, in behaving animals, SCIN pauses are not always preceded by a burst of spikes.
evidence: This is established knowledge from in vivo studies.

claim: Significant variability has been observed in the phasic responses of TANs and SCINs to reward-related stimuli in behaving animals.
source: Significant variability has been observed in the phasic responses of TANs (Zhang and Cragg, 2017) and SCINs (Duhne et al., 2024) to reward-related stimuli in behaving animals, which appears to depend on multiple factors, including striatal location and whether outcomes are appetitive or aversive.
evidence: This is supported by citations to prior work.

claim: The ex vivo model successfully reproduces the disappearance of the pause response in TANs following the induction of parkinsonism in monkeys.
source: While our ex vivo model may not fully capture the complexity of these responses, it successfully reproduces a key feature: the disappearance of the pause response in TANs following the induction of parkinsonism in monkeys.
evidence: This is supported by experimental data in the manuscript and comparison to prior in vivo work.

claim: Recent in vivo studies showed anticorrelated changes of DA and ACh striatal levels during rewarded tasks and spontaneous behavior.
source: Recent in vivo studies showed anticorrelated changes of DA and ACh striatal levels, not only during rewarded tasks but also during spontaneous behavior (Chantranupong et al., 2023; Krok et al., 2023).
evidence: This is supported by citations to recent studies.

claim: Constitutive ablation of D2Rs from cholinergic neurons disrupts the anticorrelated DA-ACh signal during specific portions of an operant task.
source: Several studies support that DA positively modulates the pause response of SCINs through D2R-mediated effects (Watanabe and Kimura, 1998; Ding et al., 2010; Kharkwal et al., 2016), and constitutive ablation of D2Rs from cholinergic neurons disrupts the anticorrelated DA-ACh signal during specific portions of an operant task (Chantranupong et al., 2023).
evidence: This is supported by citation to prior work.

claim: Striatal ACh transients persist and even increase after blockade of striatal DA receptors or lesion of nigrostriatal neurons.
source: However, striatal ACh transients persist and even increase after blockade of striatal DA receptors or lesion of nigrostriatal neurons, while they are reduced after intrastriatal infusion of glutamate receptor antagonists (Krok et al., 2023).
evidence: This is supported by citation to prior work.

claim: Slow variations of striatal glutamate, rather than DA, control ACh release from SCINs at the space and timescales resolved by fiber photometry.
source: Although these findings suggest that slow variations of striatal glutamate, rather than DA, control ACh release from SCINs at the space and timescales resolved by fiber photometry (Krok et al., 2023), they do not rule out a fine dopaminergic regulation of phasic SCIN responses to glutamatergic inputs, which could be embedded within broader modulations of DA and ACh levels.
evidence: This is supported by citation to prior work and inference.

claim: Endogenous activation of D2R modulates the pause induced by thalamic afferents in SCINs.
source: Our ex vivo data support that endogenous activation of D2R modulates the pause induced by thalamic afferents in SCINs.
evidence: This is supported by experimental data in the manuscript.

claim: Ambient DA in the slice does not modulate SCIN activity through D5Rs.
source: Moreover, we found that ambient DA in the slice does not modulate SCIN activity through D5Rs, but pharmacological stimulation of D1/D5Rs markedly inhibited the pause response, likely through inhibitory effects of D5Rs on Kv1 channels.
evidence: This is supported by experimental data in the manuscript.

claim: Pharmacological stimulation of D1/D5Rs markedly inhibited the pause response, likely through inhibitory effects of D5Rs on Kv1 channels.
source: Moreover, we found that ambient DA in the slice does not modulate SCIN activity through D5Rs, but pharmacological stimulation of D1/D5Rs markedly inhibited the pause response, likely through inhibitory effects of D5Rs on Kv1 channels.
evidence: This is supported by experimental data in the manuscript and inference from prior work.

claim: Kv1 channels are necessary for the expression of the pause response in SCINs of adult mice.
source: Overall, our data show that, in physiological conditions, Kv1 channels are necessary for the expression of the pause response in SCINs of adult mice, and that the pause can be modulated by D5Rs in addition to D2Rs.
evidence: This is supported by experimental data in the manuscript.

claim: The pause can be modulated by D5Rs in addition to D2Rs.
source: Overall, our data show that, in physiological conditions, Kv1 channels are necessary for the expression of the pause response in SCINs of adult mice, and that the pause can be modulated by D5Rs in addition to D2Rs.
evidence: This is supported by experimental data in the manuscript.

claim: D5R modulation may be relevant under conditions of phasic DA release producing synaptic concentrations of DA capable of activating the low-affinity D5Rs.
source: This D5R modulation may be relevant under conditions of phasic DA release producing synaptic concentrations of DA capable of activating the low-affinity D5Rs (Figure 6F).
evidence: This is speculative reasoning based on the experimental findings.

claim: Learning deficits are believed to play a role in the development of Parkinson's disease symptoms.
source: Learning deficits are believed to play a role in the development of Parkinson's disease symptoms.
evidence: This is established knowledge about Parkinson's disease.

claim: Practice worsens the performance of previously learned motor skills in parkinsonian mice.
source: A recent study demonstrates that practice worsens the performance of previously learned motor skills in parkinsonian mice, while practice combined with therapeutic doses of L-DOPA prevents skill deterioration (Cheung et al., 2023).
evidence: This is supported by citation to a recent study.

claim: Practice combined with therapeutic doses of L-DOPA prevents skill deterioration in parkinsonian mice.
source: A recent study demonstrates that practice worsens the performance of previously learned motor skills in parkinsonian mice, while practice combined with therapeutic doses of L-DOPA prevents skill deterioration (Cheung et al., 2023).
evidence: This is supported by citation to a recent study.

claim: SCIN dysfunction may contribute to learning deficits in parkinsonian animals.
source: While this learning deficit may be due to the loss of DA, a possible contribution of SCIN dysfunction cannot be dismissed given that, in parkinsonian monkeys, the pause response of presumptive SCINs is lost and can be partially restored with apomorphine (Aosaki et al., 1994a).
evidence: This is speculative reasoning based on prior work and the experimental findings.

claim: The Kv1 current is diminished in parkinsonian mice.
source: We reported that the Kv1 current is diminished in parkinsonian mice and further suppressed 24 hr after the termination of a dyskinetogenic L-DOPA treatment (Tubert et al., 2016; Paz et al., 2022).
evidence: This is supported by citations to prior work by the authors.

claim: The pause that follows a burst of spikes induced by stimulation of thalamostriatal afferents is markedly diminished in parkinsonian dyskinetic mice.
source: Consistent with a key role of this current in pause generation, we find that the pause that follows a burst of spikes induced by stimulation of thalamostriatal afferents in our ex vivo preparation is markedly diminished in this animal model.
evidence: This is supported by experimental data in the manuscript.

claim: Suppression of the SCIN Kv1 current in dyskinetic mice is caused by sustained cAMP signaling, likely due to enhanced ligand-independent activity of D5Rs.
source: Importantly, in previous work, we reported that suppression of the SCIN Kv1 current in dyskinetic mice is caused by sustained cAMP signaling, likely due to enhanced ligand-independent activity of D5Rs, as demonstrated by showing that inverse agonists of D5Rs acutely restore the Kv1 current (Paz et al., 2022).
evidence: This is supported by citation to prior work by the authors.

claim: Inverse agonists of D5Rs acutely restore the Kv1 current in dyskinetic mice.
source: Importantly, in previous work, we reported that suppression of the SCIN Kv1 current in dyskinetic mice is caused by sustained cAMP signaling, likely due to enhanced ligand-independent activity of D5Rs, as demonstrated by showing that inverse agonists of D5Rs acutely restore the Kv1 current (Paz et al., 2022).
evidence: This is supported by citation to prior work by the authors.

claim: Clozapine is an atypical antipsychotic that behaves as an inverse agonist of D5Rs in the absence of an agonist.
source: In the current study, we find that clozapine, an atypical antipsychotic that behaves as an inverse agonist of D5Rs in the absence of an agonist (Zhang et al., 2014), reinstates the pause response of SCINs in OFF L-DOPA dyskinetic mice.
evidence: This is supported by citation to prior work.

claim: Clozapine reinstates the pause response of SCINs in OFF L-DOPA dyskinetic mice.
source: In the current study, we find that clozapine, an atypical antipsychotic that behaves as an inverse agonist of D5Rs in the absence of an agonist (Zhang et al., 2014), reinstates the pause response of SCINs in OFF L-DOPA dyskinetic mice.
evidence: This is supported by experimental data in the manuscript.

claim: The prototypical D1/D5R antagonist SCH23390 lacks inverse agonist activity on these receptors.
source: Although clozapine also has D1/D5R antagonist properties, these effects would not manifest when DA has been depleted, as is the case in the OFF L-DOPA condition. Consistently, the prototypical D1/D5R antagonist SCH23390, which lacks inverse agonist activity on these receptors (Zhang et al., 2014; Tiberi and Caron, 1994), neither reinstates the pause response nor alters SCIN spontaneous firing.
evidence: This is supported by citations to prior work.

claim: SCH23390 neither reinstates the pause response nor alters SCIN spontaneous firing in dyskinetic mice.
source: Although clozapine also has D1/D5R antagonist properties, these effects would not manifest when DA has been depleted, as is the case in the OFF L-DOPA condition. Consistently, the prototypical D1/D5R antagonist SCH23390, which lacks inverse agonist activity on these receptors (Zhang et al., 2014; Tiberi and Caron, 1994), neither reinstates the pause response nor alters SCIN spontaneous firing.
evidence: This is supported by experimental data in the manuscript.

claim: SCH23390 blocks clozapine's effect, supporting the conclusion that clozapine restores the pause response by reducing ligand-independent D5R activity.
source: However, SCH23390 blocks clozapine's effect, supporting the conclusion that clozapine restores the pause response by reducing ligand-independent D5R activity.
evidence: This is supported by experimental data in the manuscript and inference.

claim: The pause reinstated by clozapine is suppressed by MgTx.
source: Remarkably, while the Kv1.3 blocker MgTx has no effect on SCINs in dyskinetic mice, as expected given the loss of Kv1 currents in this animal model (Paz et al., 2022), the pause reinstated by clozapine is suppressed by MgTx.
evidence: This is supported by experimental data in the manuscript.

claim: D5R inverse agonists reinstate the Kv1 current in dyskinetic mice.
